title: Family of man who died in police incident demand accountability, end to "systemic racism" in policing
article: Family and friends of a man who died after an incident involving Winnipeg Police last month spoke out for the first time this week, and said they are demanding accountability, while also demanding police services take steps to stamp out issues of "systemic racism."

"We implore society to recognize the need for police reform to address the systemic biases and excessive use of force that affect marginalized communities," an emotional Brian Wood, the father of 35-year-old James Wood, said during a Friday media conference in Winnipeg, while Brian's wife Carol stood by his side.

"Losing a child is something no parent can truly prepare for, but losing a child to a violent encounter with law enforcement amplifies the pain. It is our duty as grieving parents to fight for accountability."

Brian said that while they seek answers, the family of James has also been dealing with "immense grief and pain" since James died in the early morning hours of Jan. 27, after an incident that is now being investigated by Manitoba's Independent Investigation Unit. (IIU)
"As parents, we are living through a nightmare that no one should ever have to experience," Brian said.

According to WPS, a woman called police on Jan. 27 seeking assistance because of what she said were concerns about her intoxicated boyfriend. She also told police that she was concerned for the safety of children who were in a suite in the 200 block of Fairlane Avenue at the time, police said.
However, soon after that call the same woman called back to say that her boyfriend had fallen down a flight of stairs from their second-floor suite, and appeared to be struggling to get back up.

When police arrived at 12:23 a.m. they found the man lying on the ground in a parking lot. A now widely-shared video shows police officer approach the man around 12:25 a.m. as he is lying down, and the man appears startled when confronted by police.

In the video, three officers seemingly pin the man to the ground and he is seen then kicking one officer. That officer is then seen taking out a baton weapon and hitting the man in the back of the leg approximately six times. Video later shows the man being shocked with what appears to be a Taser.
Video also shows at least five police officers later lifting the then-handcuffed man, who at that point appeared incapacitated, and carrying his mostly limp body to a police cruiser.
The man was rushed to Grace Hospital and later transferred to Health Sciences Centre where he later passed away.

Hilda Anderson-Pyrz, a relative of James Wood, and a longtime advocate for the rights of Indigenous people, spoke at Friday's media conference, and said she continues to be "horrified" by what she saw in video of the incident.

She said she and many others believe there needs to be wide-scale reform in how police deal with incidents that may be escalating, and in how police and society as a whole deal with and interact with Indigenous people.
"This country needs the political will to create transformative change so that, as Indigenous people, when we're calling on services or supports we don't die," Anderson said.

"Our human rights are continuously violated and not upheld as Indigenous people in this country. We continue to experience loss after loss, tragedy after tragedy and our hearts are broken continuously."

Anderson said she will now call for a number of steps to be taken, including asking that legislation be enacted that bans discriminatory practices and racial profiling in police forces, and new mandates that would see all police officers use body camera technology.
She also wants body cam footage stored by police services, a national database created that would track police misconduct, and more done to to hire officers from "diverse background."
"We demand accountability from those who have sworn to protect and serve. The time for silence and complacency is over," Anderson-Pyrz said.

On Friday, Shirley Ducharme, the chief of Wood's home community of O-Pipon-Na-Piwin Cree Nation, said she believes police forces need more training to properly deal with escalating situations, and situation involving Indigenous people and communities.

"The lack of understanding, empathy and knowledge about our cultures and histories contributes to the perpetuation of harmful stereotypes and biases," Ducharme said. "Training would help officers de-escalate situations involving people in crisis, preventing unnecessary use of force.
"This is not an isolated incident; it is a deeply-rooted problem that requires immediate attention and comprehensive solutions."
As of Friday the IIU, an independent police watch dog that investigates all serious matters involving police in Manitoba continues to investigate the events surrounding James Wood's death.
The Winnipeg Sun reached out to Winnipeg Police for a response or comment on Friday but so far has not received a response.
- Dave Baxter is a Local Journalism Initiative reporter who works out of the Winnipeg Sun. The Local Journalism Initiative is funded by the Government of Canada.
